name: Prompting and Task Execution
summary: Writing requests that get useful results from Claude for business and technical work, breaking big jobs into steps, and adapting to the type of task.
keyIdeas: Say who it is for, what you want, what good looks like, and any constraints.
Give relevant background and examples; say what format you want.
Break complex requests into steps or ask Claude to plan first.
Iterate: react to the first draft instead of rewriting everything.
Match the approach to the task: analysis, writing, coding and brainstorming need different instructions.
traps: Asking in one vague sentence and blaming the model.
Pasting a huge task with no structure.
Starting over each time instead of refining.

name: Output Evaluation and Validation
summary: Checking what Claude produces: accuracy, completeness, hallucinations and bias, and deciding when a human must verify.
keyIdeas: Fluent does not mean correct. Check facts, numbers, names and citations against reliable sources.
Hallucinations are confident but unsupported statements; ask for sources and verify them.
Consistency checks: compare against your material, or ask again a different way.
The higher the stakes (legal, medical, financial, public), the more human verification you need.
Edit and adapt the output for the audience; choose the format that suits the use.
traps: Treating a citation as real because it looks formatted.
Sending output to a client without reading it.

name: Product and Model Selection
summary: Choosing the right Claude product feature and model for a task, and understanding context and memory limits.
keyIdeas: Faster, lighter models suit simple, high-volume work; more capable models suit complex reasoning; balanced models cover most tasks.
Different products suit different jobs: chat, Projects for ongoing work, Artifacts for documents and apps, coding tools for developers.
A conversation has a finite context window; very long chats can lose detail.
A new chat does not remember an old one unless memory or Projects provide the context.
traps: Using the most powerful model for every small task.
Expecting a new chat to know last week's chat.

name: Workflow Integration and Solution Design
summary: Using Claude to analyse needs, plan, and improve processes, and explaining its value and limits honestly.
keyIdeas: Start with a specific task that is repetitive, text-heavy and low-risk.
Keep a person in the loop where judgement or accountability matters.
Pilot with real users, measure time saved and quality, then expand.
Be clear with stakeholders about what Claude does well and where it needs checks.
traps: Promising that AI will replace the whole process.
Skipping a pilot and rolling out to everyone.

name: Configuration and Knowledge Management
summary: Setting Claude up for repeat work: Projects, instructions, uploaded knowledge and connectors.
keyIdeas: A Project keeps instructions and knowledge together for a topic or team.
Good instructions are specific: role, audience, tone, format, and what to do when unsure.
Keep knowledge files current, named clearly and relevant; remove outdated ones.
Connectors let Claude use tools and data you authorise; review what access you grant.
traps: Leaving outdated documents in the project.
Granting broad access to a connector without thinking.

name: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use
summary: Using Claude appropriately: which tasks fit, how to protect sensitive data, following your organisation's rules, and thinking about ethics.
keyIdeas: Follow your organisation's AI policy and use approved tools and accounts.
Do not enter confidential, personal or regulated data unless policy and the tool's protections allow it.
Be transparent when AI helped produce work, when your context requires it.
Watch for bias, and do not use AI as the sole decision-maker for consequential decisions about people.
Be accountable: you own what you send.
traps: Pasting customer records into a personal account.
Hiding AI use where disclosure is required.

name: Troubleshooting and Optimization
summary: Diagnosing weak results and improving your approach and workflows.
keyIdeas: Diagnose first: was the request unclear, was context missing, or is the task wrong for AI?
Change one thing at a time and compare.
Give feedback that says what is wrong and what to do instead.
Save prompts that work as templates; standardise repeated workflows.
Start a fresh chat with a summary when a long conversation drifts.
traps: Repeating the same request and hoping.
Rewriting everything at once so you can't tell what helped.
